title: Climate change impacting skin health, disproportionately burdening lower-income countries
content: A major international study spanning 136 countries found that over 40 per cent of countries worldwide reported climate-related changes in the prevalence and severity of skin diseases with lower-income countries disproportionately affected. The study was presented at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 in Vienna. Representatives from 194 World Health Organization (WHO) member countries were invited to participate in the Global Access to Skin Health Observatory (SkinObservatory) study, a collaboration between the International League of Dermatological Societies (ILDS) and L’Oréal Dermatological Beauty. The Skin Observatory maps dermatologist distribution, workforce gaps and barriers to care across WHO member states, generating evidence to identify where needs are greatest and support stronger, more equitable skin health services. Participants shared insights on climate impacts and the prevalence of climate change-related skin diseases in their countries. Data was collected from 136 countries. Overall, 42.6 per cent reported changes in the prevalence and / or severity of skin disease due to climate change, with significant differences according to income level. More than half of low-income (55.6 per cent) and lower-middle-income countries (52.5 per cent) reported climate-related changes in skin disease, compared with 43.8 per cent of upper-middle-income and 28.3 per cent of high-income countries. Geographical differences were also substantial, with changes most frequently reported in the western Pacific region (64.7 per cent), followed by the eastern Mediterranean and south-east Asian regions (60 per cent each), compared with 16.1 per cent in the European region. In the African Region, 42.9 per cent of respondents were unsure about the impact of climate change on skin disease. This highlights gaps in surveillance and evidence. Among the 58 countries reporting climate-associated effects on skin disease, 81 per cent reported increases in heat rashes and 75.9 per cent in inflammatory skin diseases. Changes in infectious diseases were reported in 62.1 per cent, with half (50.0%) reporting changes in vector-borne diseases. “The most important finding from our study is that climate change is already associated with negative impacts on skin disease, and these effects disproportionately burden lower-income settings,” said study author Dr Esther Freeman , Harvard Medical School. “We often think about the effects of extreme weather on heatstroke, cardiovascular problems and respiratory diseases, but the skin is our front line to climate change," Dr Freeman added.

title: Nepal hit again by devastating flash floods
content: Disaster struck Nepal again as a torrent of mud, rocks and debris tore through villages in Nepal’s Himalayan foothills on October 11. Dozens of homes and several bridges were swept away and at least five people are reported to be missing. The flash flood struck the Budhi Gandaki River, a tributary of the Trishuli River in Gorkha district, around 100 kilometres west of Kathmandu. Preliminary assessments by Nepal’s disaster authorities and the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development suggest that a landslide blocked the river upstream, creating a temporary barrier that later gave way and unleashed a sudden surge downstream. The precise cause is still being assessed. Almost 45 houses were swept away, with the flood also damaging three hydropower projects and four bridges. Floodwaters also damaged the construction site and equipment of the under-construction 341-megawatt Budhi Gandaki hydropower project, along with electricity and telecommunications infrastructure. Authorities issued mobile phone alerts and urged residents downstream, including those along the Trishuli and Narayani river systems, to move to safer areas. The Nepali Army rescued 95 people, including nine foreign nationals. According to Nepal’s disaster management authority, 437 security personnel had been mobilised for rescue operations as of Sunday. The disaster comes as Nepal continues to grapple with the aftermath of deadly flooding in August, which killed more than 1,400 people and over 5000 missing.

title: September 2026 second hottest on record
content: September 2026 was the second hottest September month on record, with global monthly average temperatures breaching 1.5°C for two consecutive months, according to the latest update from Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), implemented by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. The average sea surface temperature (SST) for oceans outside the polar regions was also the highest on record, as El Nino conditions in the Equatorial Pacific Ocean keep intensifying as one of the strongest El Nino events , according to C3S. Global average temperature for September 2026 was 16.27°C, which was 0.82°C above the average during 1991-2020 and 1.63°C above the pre-industrial (1850-1900) levels. The month was 0.11°C cooler than September 2023, making it the second-warmest on record. September is the second consecutive month to record global temperature anomaly above 1.5°C, after August global temperatures were 1.65°C above the pre industrial levels. August 2026 was the joint hottest month on record, according to C3S. Many regions around the world were drier than normal. “Drier-than-average regions included much of southern and northeastern North America, the Maghreb, part of the Horn of Africa, Siberia, large parts of central Asia, Pakistan, parts of China, parts of South America, and southeastern Australia,” according to a press release by C3S. In contrast “wetter-than-average regions included large parts of the US and Canada, parts of northern Russia, central Asia north of the Indian subcontinent, eastern China, Japan, Chile, southern Argentina and southeastern Brazil as well as southernmost Africa and western Australia”, as per C3S. In several regions, heavy precipitation led to floods. The SSTs outside the polar regions (60°S–60°N) created a new record in September with an average value of 21.05°C, going past the previous record of 20.92°C set in 2023. “The monthly SST for the Nino 3.4 region (the ocean region used to monitor El Nino conditions) reached an all-time high of 29.70°C in September, exceeding the peak values of the previous very strong El Nino events of 1982 / 1983, 1997 / 1998 and 2015 / 2016 and underscoring the exceptional intensity of the current El Nino,” according to C3S press release. “September was the second warmest on record globally, with exceptionally high temperatures experienced again across parts of Europe after an extreme summer,” said Carlo Buontempo, director of C3S, in the press release. “We are in a new run of months above 1.5°C, and with a strong El Nino still intensifying it is likely to last into 2027. Crossing the Paris Agreement's long-term limit is only a matter of time,” he added.

title: Daily weather tracker: Northeast monsoon set to arrive in South India as storms, strong winds, hail threaten northern states
content: Northeast monsoon approaches South India: Rainfall likely within two to three days as a developing Bay of Bengal low-pressure system influences weather. Hailstorm alert for Northern states: Delhi, Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh may experience hailstorms, lightning and gusty winds reaching 50 kilometres per hour on October 14–15. Thunderstorms expected across several states: Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jammu and Kashmir, Ladakh and northeastern states may witness rainfall, lightning and strong winds. Rajkot records season’s high temperature: Gujarat’s Rajkot recorded 39.8°C on October 12, while Haryana’s Karnal registered a minimum temperature of 15°C. Farmers face crop damage risks: Strong winds and hailstorms threaten standing crops, banana and papaya plantations, prompting farmers to monitor official weather warnings and take precautions. India is bracing for another significant shift in weather patterns, with thunderstorms, strong winds and possible hailstorms expected across parts of northern India on October 14 and 15. At the same time, the northeast monsoon is likely to make its onset over southern India within the next two to three days, bringing fresh rainfall prospects to several states. According to the latest weather update issued on the morning of October 13, 2026, a western disturbance over northwestern Uttar Pradesh, accompanied by an upper-air cyclonic circulation and a trough in the westerlies, is influencing atmospheric conditions across northern India. The developing weather systems could trigger thunderstorms, lightning and gusty winds, raising concerns among farmers and residents in vulnerable areas. Delhi, Haryana, Punjab and Chandigarh are likely to experience heightened weather activity over the coming days. The India Meteorological Department has indicated the possibility of hailstorms in isolated parts of these regions on October 14 and 15, accompanied by lightning and strong winds reaching speeds of 40 to 50 kilometres per hour. The impact is expected to vary across locations, with adverse conditions likely to remain confined to certain pockets. Nevertheless, strong winds could break tree branches, uproot vulnerable trees and damage electricity and communication lines. Hailstorms may also affect standing crops, particularly those susceptible to sudden weather disturbances. Residents have been advised to remain alert to changing weather conditions and follow official forecasts, especially during thunderstorms. Unsettled weather is also expected in several other parts of the country. Parts of Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jammu and Kashmir, and Ladakh may experience rainfall, lightning and gusty winds reaching 30 to 40 kilometres per hour. Some areas of Andhra Pradesh could also witness strong surface winds. Isolated thunderstorms and lightning are possible in Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Mahe, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal. These conditions could bring brief spells of rain and temporary disruptions to daily activities. Meanwhile, parts of Konkan and Goa may continue to experience hot and humid conditions, adding to discomfort despite the changing weather elsewhere. The contrasting conditions underline the diversity of India's seasonal transition, with some regions facing storm-related risks while others continue to experience above-normal temperatures. As the southwest monsoon's withdrawal progresses, the northeast monsoon is expected to begin over southern India within the next two to three days. The weather department has also indicated that the remaining parts of the country could witness the withdrawal of the southwest monsoon during this period. An upper-air cyclonic circulation persists over the South Andaman Sea and neighbouring areas. Under its influence, a low-pressure area is likely to develop over the southeastern Bay of Bengal around October 13. This developing system could influence weather conditions across southern India in the coming days, potentially strengthening rainfall activity in parts of the region. The onset of the northeast monsoon is particularly important for southern peninsular India, where seasonal rainfall plays a crucial role in agriculture, water availability and reservoir replenishment. Temperature readings recorded on October 12 highlight the contrasting weather conditions prevailing across the country. Rajkot in Gujarat registered the highest maximum temperature at 39.8 degrees Celsius, indicating persistent heat in parts of western India. In the plains, Karnal in Haryana recorded a minimum temperature of 15 degrees Celsius, reflecting comparatively cooler night-time conditions. Maximum temperatures remained considerably above normal in parts of coastal Karnataka and some other regions. Parts of Assam and Meghalaya also recorded minimum temperatures significantly above their seasonal averages. The approaching weather disturbances could pose challenges for farmers, particularly those with standing crops and horticultural plantations. Strong winds and hailstones can damage crops, break stems and affect agricultural produce, potentially causing financial losses. Banana and papaya plants are especially vulnerable to strong winds, while fruit orchards and other horticultural crops may also suffer damage under severe conditions. Farmers and rural residents should monitor official weather bulletins, avoid working in exposed fields during thunderstorms and seek shelter in safe buildings when lightning or hail begins. People should also stay away from isolated trees and unsecured electrical structures during strong winds. With the northeast monsoon approaching and storm activity expected in northern India, the next several days could bring sharply contrasting weather conditions across the country.

title: International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction: Resilience starts at home, but only if land beneath is secure, people prepared
content: In Nepal’s Nuwakot district this year, a turquoise house became an unlikely symbol of hope. A glacial flash flood swept away the buildings around it. The house, built with a reinforced concrete frame on a bedrock foundation, stayed standing and sheltered its occupants. The image fits this year’s theme for the International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction on October 13, 2026: “Resilience Starts at Home.” The UN Office for Disaster Risk Reduction (UNDRR) calls the home the place where disasters are most acutely felt and where resilience must begin. But a miracle house is no model for the millions of families whose homes stand on riverbanks and riverbeds. Read closely, the theme has three components. The house must be resilient. The land beneath it must be safe and secure, with a patta (land title) for the people who live on it. And the people inside, especially the most vulnerable, must be prepared. Remove any one and the home is not resilient. Satyabhama Mallick, 61, a widow from a Scheduled Caste community, has lived alone in Rahania village of Bhadrak district, Odisha, for nearly three decades. Her daughter is married and lives elsewhere. She survives on a widow pension and ration grain, with no stable livelihood, savings or alternative shelter. This year’s monsoon floods destroyed her house. Rebuilding is not simply a matter of bricks and roofing sheets. The land she has occupied for about 30 years is recorded as anabadi , uncultivated government land, which leaves her eligibility for housing reconstruction support in doubt. Too frail to reach the relief distribution point, she was visited at home by an ActionAid team, and on 20 August received a grocery kit and a shelter-cum-hygiene kit. They mattered. But she now lives in a thatch structure that is barely holding together, and the question of her land is unresolved. Relief is a bridge, not a destination. Her case exposes a question disaster policy often skips: what makes a house a home? A house can survive a flood and a family can still lose their home if their right to the land is uncertain. Land that is cheap or available is often land exposed to hazard. The same insecurity that pushes the poorest towards riverbanks and marginal plots later keeps them out of reconstruction assistance. Odisha’s Revenue and Disaster Management Minister told the Assembly on 24 September that this year’s floods affected 32,48,943 people in 22 districts and damaged 18,076 houses, with ₹33 crore released as housing assistance. But a damaged house must first be identified, the family assessed, eligibility established, land found where needed and aid delivered. For a family without secure land, every stage is another place to fall through. The scale of the land problem is documented. A 2024 audit by the Comptroller and Auditor General found 46,949 landless households on Odisha’s PMAY-G Permanent Waiting List as of February 2021: eligible for a house, with nowhere to build it. The survey meant to identify homestead-less families had last been done in 2018. The state has since moved. The Awaas+ 2024 survey identified about 2.01 lakh landless households among roughly 37.89 lakh surveyed. In late 2025, Collectors were told to give landless families priority in house-site allotment, and block officials and tehsildars were asked to meet on the first Saturday of every month to settle pending land issues. The Vasundhara framework also allows the state to buy private land for homestead-less families where government land is unavailable. Implementation is the test. As of September, the Permanent Waiting List was still to be prepared, and the government told the Assembly that no houses had been sanctioned under PMAY-G in Odisha in 2025-26 or 2026-27. Land allocation should not wait for sanctions. A strong house on secure land still fails the person who cannot get out in time, or whom nobody thinks to look for. Preparedness matters most for older persons, persons with disabilities, single women and widows. UNDRR’s theme itself calls for stronger household preparedness and for early warnings that reach everyone at risk. The global gap is wide. UNDRR’s 2023 survey of persons with disabilities found that 84 per cent had no personal preparedness plan, up from 71 per cent in 2013, and reported that in some cases persons with disabilities die in disasters at two to four times the rate of others. These figures are global, not India-specific, but they describe the gap local preparedness must close. Closing it takes two things. The first is community preparedness training that includes vulnerable people and their families, not only able-bodied volunteers: drills, known evacuation routes and shelters, a plan for who helps whom, and safekeeping of documents, including land records. The second is training first responders, from village volunteers and Gram Panchayat members to disaster management committees and officials, to identify and prioritise these groups for evacuation, relief and rehabilitation. That needs vulnerability lists updated before every monsoon, not names collected after a disaster. The Humanitarian Schools run by ActionAid and other agencies aim to build exactly this capacity among communities and local responders. They deserve to be strengthened: wider coverage of flood-prone villages, refresher training before each monsoon, a firmer focus on inclusion, and formal links with Gram Panchayats and district disaster management authorities so that what is learnt becomes part of the official plan. First, landless households identified through Awaas+ or any other scheme should receive house sites without waiting for sanctions. Housing assistance leads to a durable home only where there is land to build on. Second, eligibility for families on government land should rest on verified long-term residence and vulnerability, within the legal framework, not on land classification alone. A technical label should not be a dead end for someone with nowhere else to go. Third, surveys of homestead-less households should be held at least once a year, so families are identified before a disaster deepens their vulnerability. Fourth, damage assessment and scheme enrolment must reach people who cannot travel to camps or block offices because of age, illness or disability, through home-based verification. Fifth, households whose homes are destroyed need polythene or tarpaulin at once, not only dry food, as a bridge until permanent housing and any land allocation come through. Finally, civil society can bridge the last mile through vulnerability surveys, case tracking and follow-up with Gram Panchayats and block administrations, and by strengthening community and first-responder training.

title: International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction: El Niño shows why household resilience must begin before disaster strikes
content: As a very strong El Niño unfolds, households are likely to absorb much of the human and economic cost through lost income, higher prices, depleted savings and mounting debt. Post-Disaster Needs Assessments from 20 countries in Asia and the Pacific show that around 40 per cent of disaster impacts occur in social and productive sectors, affecting housing, health, education and livelihoods. The article argues that governments must turn accurate El Niño forecasts into actionable guidance for farmers, urban residents and small businesses. Stronger household preparedness, concessional finance, insurance support and climate-responsive social protection can help families withstand shocks before they become disasters. As a very strong El Niño unfolds, increasing the risk of severe weather into 2027 , attention is rightly focused on whether governments have the fiscal capacity to sustain a prolonged response and recovery. Yet one important question receives less attention: who ultimately pays most of the disaster bill? Households absorb much of the human and economic cost of disasters. Past El Niño events have shown how quickly climate shocks can cascade into livelihood impacts. Families pay through lost income, higher food and energy prices, mounting debt, depleted savings, disruption to work and schooling, and reduced spending on health and education. This is not anecdotal. Post-Disaster Needs Assessments from 20 countries in Asia and the Pacific show that approximately 40 per cent of disaster impacts occur in social and productive sectors, affecting housing, health, education and subsistence livelihoods. When disasters strike, households typically rely on a mixture of coping mechanisms: drawing down savings, borrowing money, receiving support from relatives or seeking government assistance. Poorer households often have fewer options and face longer recoveries. The 2015-2016 El Niño illustrated these patterns, causing crop losses, food insecurity and malnutrition across Asia and the Pacific, with impacts persisting for months after the event ended. This year’s International Day for Disaster Risk Reduction carries a timely message: Resilience Starts at Home. While households bear the greatest burden of preparing for, withstanding and recovering from disasters, governments have a crucial role in helping them build that capacity. In the context of the current El Niño, three interventions deserve particular attention. El Niño forecasts have become increasingly accurate, with at least six months of lead time before major impacts on weather and seasons emerge. The challenge is to ensure that scientific information translates into actionable guidance. Public trust is critical. During the 2015-2016 El Niño, governments remained the primary source of information on El Niño and its impacts. Trusted, timely and practical public communication is therefore more important than ever. Farmers need guidance on crop selection and planting schedules. Urban residents need information on heat risks and possible disruptions to transport, water, electricity and public services. Small businesses need information that helps them manage supply-chain disruptions and operational risks. But access to information is only as valuable as the capacity to act on it. Climate-risk information alone is often insufficient if households lack the means to respond. Supporting households therefore requires coordinated action across government institutions. For example, when forecasts indicate drought conditions, farmers may need to switch to more drought-tolerant crops. Doing so often requires support from agricultural and water management agencies, cooperatives and extension services to access farm inputs, credit and markets. Households often underinvest in resilience because the costs are immediate while the benefits may not materialise for years. Setting aside money for water storage facilities, home retrofits, insurance coverage, back-up power systems and other risk-reducing measures can be difficult when household budgets are already stretched. Poor and vulnerable households may also face barriers in accessing finance, risk information and other resources needed to take preventive action. Public policy can create an enabling environment for households to act before shocks occur. Insurance support, concessional finance, risk-informed advisory services and public investment in climate-resilient infrastructure can make risk reduction more affordable and compelling. Well-designed incentives, as part of broader household risk-management strategies, are particularly important for families that depend disproportionately on climate-sensitive livelihoods and lack savings, remittances or other financial buffers. Even with better information and stronger mitigation measures, the unprecedented intensity of the current El Niño could overwhelm some households. For these families, social protection functions as a form of disaster finance. Well-designed social protection systems reduce the need for harmful coping strategies such as selling productive assets, withdrawing children from school or cutting essential health spending. Shock-responsive cash transfers and adaptive social assistance programmes can help households absorb temporary disruptions while also reducing poverty and inequality . Climate shocks affect households differently. While lower-income rural households are disproportionately affected by climate hazards overall, urban households can also experience rising food prices, heat stress, service disruptions and higher living costs. Effective resilience policies need to reflect the different ways in which climate shocks are experienced across households and communities, including the distinct challenges faced by women and vulnerable groups. This year’s IDDRR theme recognises that resilience ultimately depends on the capacity of households to anticipate risks, absorb shocks and recover with dignity. Public policy plays a critical role in building that capacity. By strengthening risk knowledge and anticipatory action, supporting household-level risk reduction and expanding climate-responsive social protection, governments can help families avoid the worst impacts, rather than simply recover after the fact. As forecasts point to an exceptionally strong El Niño extending into 2027, the risks are unfolding against the long-term backdrop of an escalating climate crisis. With 85 per cent of people in Asia and the Pacific exposed to multiple climate-related risks, building resilience at home is not just an El Niño response. It is one of the smartest investments governments can make for an increasingly unpredictable future.
